**Where we got to — the story so far.** This is the fourth document, written
Wednesday evening. It pulls together the answers from the first three into one
page, and every number in it is computed from the data in this document, so
nothing can drift from the truth. The full working for each answer is in the
document listed beside it.

| # | Document | Question | Answer in one line |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `01-qc.qmd` | Is the data good enough to analyse? | Yes — all six files agree; three flags to carry forward |
| 2 | `02-community-composition.qmd` | Do the arms differ in community *composition*? | No evidence — arm explains ~3% of distances, p = 0.15 |
| 3 | `03-bv-by-arm.qmd` | Is **BV** more common in one arm? | No evidence — rates 49% / 36% / 38%, p = 0.45 |
| 4 | this one | — | The two answers, side by side, with what we can and cannot conclude |

## The study

Ninety-three people, one vaginal sample each, randomly assigned to one of
three contraceptive methods. We analyse the microbiome (134 observed species
after dropping the 86 never seen), the RNAseq table, the cytokines, and the
clinical labels (Nugent score, BV).

```{r}
#| label: setup
source(here::here("R/count_tables.R"))
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(microViz)
  library(phyloseq)
  library(vegan)
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)
})
set.seed(2026)

d <- read_counts("group_b")
meta <- d$metadata
ps <- as_counts("group_b", "microbiome", min_count = 1, min_samples = 1)
ps   # 134 species x 93 samples
```

## Answer 1: the arms do not differ in community composition

Full working in `02-community-composition.qmd`.

"Community composition" = the whole species profile of a sample at once.
PERMANOVA asks: do samples from the same arm sit closer together than samples
from different arms? R² = the share of variation the grouping explains.

```{r}
#| label: answer1
meta_ps <- as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame")
dist_bray <- ps |>
  tax_transform("compositional") |>
  dist_calc("bray") |>
  (\(x) x@dist)()

m2 <- adonis2(dist_bray ~ arm + rnaseq_batch,
              data = meta_ps, by = "margin", permutations = 999)
m3 <- adonis2(dist_bray ~ arm + rnaseq_batch + nugent,
              data = meta_ps, by = "margin", permutations = 999)

knitr::kable(tibble(
  Question = c(
    "Does arm explain community composition? (primary model)",
    "Does arm explain it after accounting for BV severity?",
    "Does sequencing batch explain it?",
    "Does BV severity (Nugent) explain it? — the positive control"
  ),
  `R2 (share of variation)` = round(c(
    m2$R2[1], m3$R2[1], m3$R2[2], m3$R2[3]
  ), 3),
  `p-value` = signif(c(
    m2[["Pr(>F)"]][[1]], m3[["Pr(>F)"]][[1]],
    m3[["Pr(>F)"]][[2]], m3[["Pr(>F)"]][[3]]
  ), 2)
))
```

**No evidence.** Arm explains about 3% of the variation, p = 0.15 — or
about 0.07 after accounting for BV severity (second row of the table):
closer to the line, still above 0.05. The same pipeline on the same samples
finds a huge real signal — **BV severity explains 24% at p = 0.001** — so the
test works; the arm signal just is not there. The answer survives a second
distance metric (Aitchison, p = 0.16), a dispersion check (equal spreads,
p = 0.76), the QC flags, and a label-shuffle null (4 of 20 random shuffles beat
the real arm R²).

## Answer 2: BV is not more common in one arm

Full working in `03-bv-by-arm.qmd`.

BV here is the clinical label: Nugent score 7–10 on Gram-stain microscopy.

```{r}
#| label: answer2
ft <- fisher.test(table(meta$arm, meta$bv))

rates <- meta |>
  count(arm, name = "people") |>
  left_join(
    meta |> filter(bv == "positive") |> count(arm, name = "bv_positive"),
    by = "arm"
  ) |>
  mutate(rate = scales::percent(bv_positive / people, accuracy = 0.1))

# The molecular second opinion: Lactobacillus-dominated or not.
lac_taxa <- d$taxonomy |> filter(Genus == "Lactobacillus") |> pull(taxon)
lac_frac <- colSums(d$species[lac_taxa, ]) / colSums(d$species)
mol <- meta |>
  mutate(community = ifelse(lac_frac[meta$sample_id] >= 0.5,
                            "lactobacillus", "anaerobe"))
ft_mol <- fisher.test(table(mol$community, mol$arm))

knitr::kable(rates)
cat("Fisher exact, clinical label: p =", signif(ft$p.value, 2), "\n")
cat("Fisher exact, molecular type: p =", signif(ft_mol$p.value, 2), "\n")
cat("Kruskal-Wallis, Nugent score by arm: p =",
    signif(kruskal.test(nugent ~ arm, meta)$p.value, 2), "\n")
```

**No evidence.** Injectable looks highest (49% vs 36% / 38%), but with 26–39
people per arm that 13-point gap is well within what chance produces
(Fisher p = 0.45). The molecular definition of "BV-ish" (anaerobe-type
community) agrees (p = 0.53), and the two definitions agree with *each other*
(37 of 39 clinical positives are anaerobe-type, p < 0.001) — so it is not a
measurement problem.

## What we can and cannot conclude

The two answers agree with each other, which is reassuring: if contraception
changed the community, composition *and* BV rates would likely both have
moved.

What we **can** say:

- No *large* difference between arms, in composition or in BV rates.
- The vaginal community in this cohort varies mostly with **BV status**
  (24% of composition variation), which is present in all three arms at
  similar rates — that is the dominant biological axis here, not
  contraception.

What we **cannot** say:

- Not "the arms are identical." With 93 people (26–39 per arm), only a
  fairly large difference had any chance of showing up: in the BV analysis,
  roughly a 36-percentage-point gap was needed for reliable detection, and the
  observed gap was 13 points. A modest real difference would have been
  invisible.
- Nothing about *change over time* — each person was sampled once, so both
  analyses compare *between* people.

The natural next questions (for tomorrow): which *individual species* differ
by arm (a DESeq2 question, untested by anything above — the community-level
test could miss a single-species shift), and the same for genes.

## How you could catch me being wrong

- **Answer 1's table** should show Nugent at R² ≈ 0.24 and arm at ≈ 0.03. If
  arm shows R² = 0.2, I have loaded the wrong dataset or the wrong model.
- **Answer 2's table** should total 93 people (39 + 28 + 26). If the three
  rates are not 48.7% / 35.7% / 38.5%, the counts and the prose disagree —
  believe the table.
- **Cross-check against the originals:** each number here also appears in the
  document it came from (`02` and `03`). If a number differs between this
  page and its source document, one of us has drifted.

## Choices made

- Computed every number live in this document rather than copying numbers from documents 02 and 03 — alternative not chosen: pasting the values in, which would silently go stale if the data changed.
- Summarised only the two primary analyses (composition and BV prevalence) — alternative not chosen: re-summarising every robustness check, which would duplicate the source documents' jobs.
- Reported the primary two-variable composition model (arm + batch, p = 0.15) as the headline, with the three-variable model (adds Nugent, p = 0.069) as the second row of the same table — alternative not chosen: picking one model and hiding the other, which would have understated how close arm comes to 0.05 once BV severity is accounted for.
- Framed the limits as "what we can / cannot conclude" rather than only the p-values — alternative not chosen: stopping at "not significant", which lets "no evidence" masquerade as "no difference".
- Named the next questions (per-species and per-gene DESeq2) at the end — alternative not chosen: leaving the summary as a dead end; naming them makes tomorrow's starting point explicit.
- Kept all 93 samples and the same filters as the source documents (134 observed species) so the numbers here match there — alternative not chosen: a stricter filter, which would make this page disagree with its own sources.
